Story
STOR-ee
noun (Millennial slang)
From Latin historia through Old French estoire, the ordinary English word for a narrative. Snapchat introduced Stories in October 2013: a sequence of photos and videos visible to friends for twenty-four hours, then gone. Instagram copied the format in August 2016, and Facebook, WhatsApp, and others followed; "post it on your story" and "did you see my story?" became everyday speech. The format favours the casual, the momentary, and the curated glimpse.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

A story, in social-media speech, is a string of photos and short videos posted for twenty-four hours and then deleted: what you ate, where you are, who you are with, a quote, a mood. It is the daily, disappearing self-portrait. The Christian observation: the format itself is a kind of parable. The story vanishes after a day, and Scripture has a word about lives that are like that: "For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away" (Jas 4:14). "We spend our years as a tale that is told" (Psa 90:9). The disappearing post is a fitting image of human transience, and it ought to make us ask what lasts. There are also two cautions. The story invites constant curation of one’s life for an audience: the highlight, the angle, the filtered moment, which can make a young person live for the post rather than the moment. And it invites constant watching of other people’s stories, which feeds comparison and envy. Christians have a better story to live in. The word story once meant history, a true account: the Chronicler refers to "the story of the prophet Iddo" (2Ch 13:22). The gospel is the true story into which our small ones are written, and it does not vanish in a day: "the word of our God shall stand for ever" (Isa 40:8). A father asks his children: are you living your life, or posting it? He teaches them to share good things, to put the phone down at the moments that matter most, and to care more about the story God is writing than the one that disappears tomorrow.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial social-media sense (Snapchat 2013; Instagram 2016) of a 24-hour disappearing post; a parable of the vapour of life (Jas 4:14), with cautions against curating life for an audience, set beside the story that stands for ever (Isa 40:8).

Decode for parents: ask your children whether they experience moments or curate them; then model putting the phone away.

Key Scripture

Jas 4:14 — "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away."

Psa 90:9 — "For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told."

2Ch 13:22 — "And the rest of the acts of Abijah, and his ways, and his sayings, are written in the story of the prophet Iddo."

Isa 40:8 — "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever."

Psa 90:12 — "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

Modern Corruption

The disappearing story trains young people to curate their lives for an audience and to watch others with envy; Scripture calls life a vapour and points to the story that stands for ever.

expand to see more

The corruption is life lived for the post. When every outing is a potential story, the question "how will this look?" sits beside every experience, and attention shifts from the people present to the people watching. Meanwhile, hours go into viewing other people’s curated days, which breeds comparison. The format is ephemeral, but the habits it forms are not.

The redemption is to number our days rightly. "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Psa 90:12). Because life is a vapour, it should be spent on what lasts: love, faithfulness, worship, the people in front of us. Teach the young to share good things gladly, to leave the phone in the pocket at the table and the graveside and the altar, and to live as characters in God’s true story, which no one can delete.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek historia (inquiry, account) → Latin historia → Old French estoire → English story → 2013 Snapchat / 2016 Instagram "Stories."
